newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Reserve Bank downplays risk of S.African downturn.
newsitem.headline: Reserve Bank downplays risk of S.African downturn.

text.p: South Africa's Reserve Bank, under pressure to cut interest rates after a surprise drop in first quarter GDP, said on Thursday it was not convinced the economy was facing an imminent downturn.

The central bank acknowledged in its Quarterly Bulletin that the 0.8 percent quarter-on-quarter annualised decline in GDP in the three months to March could signal that an upturn which started in 1993 might be drawing to a close.
The compositive coincident business cycle indicator had also been showing a gradually downward tendency since mid-1995.

But these signs of an imminent downturn in the business cycle were contradicted by the relative strength of output growth in the secondary sectors of the economy during the first quarter, the Bank said.

"Manufacturing output, especially, not only maintained the upward momentum that had developed since the final quarter of 1996, but even accelerated quite substantially in the first quarter of 1997," it said.

"What is more, the recent generally upward trend in the backlog of unfilled orders might have been pointing towards a continuation of manufacturing output growth in the remainder of 1997. It is conceivable that the resilience of manufacturing output growth might be a stabilising factor in 1997."

The decline in first quarter GDP, which took economists by surprise, was essentially due to a drop in agriculture as the industry adjusted to more "normal" weather conditions after excellent rains in 1996.
The bank also noted that GDP in the first quarter of 1997 was still some 2-1/2 percent higher than in the first quarter of 1996.

The decline in first quarter GDP coincided with a further decline in gross domestic expenditure which fell by a seasonally adjusted and annualised rate of 0.5 percent. However, this was less than the declines of two percent recorded in both the fourth and third quarters of 1996.

Private consumption expenditure, which had already slowed down from an annualised rate of increase of four percent in the second quarter of 1996 to 2.5 percent in the fourth quarter, declined further to only 0.5 percent in the first quarter of 1997. Household expenditure on durable consumer goods fell by 2.5 percent.
Consumption expenditure by government increased, however, growing at 5.5 percent in the first quarter of 1997 from 4.5 percent in the last quarter of 1996.
Growth in gross domestic fixed investment fell to two percent in the first quarter from 2.5 percent in the fourth quarter of last year and eight percent in the first quarter of 1996.
Private sector investment also increased by a meagre two percent in the three months to March after an average six percent increase per quarter in 1996.
"This was, nevertheless, the 16th consecutive quarterly rise in real fixed investment in the private sector," the bank noted.

The Reserve Bank added that the strengthening of output growth in the non-agricultural sectors of the economy in the second half of 1996 led to a 0.4 percent increase in total employment in the formal non-agricultural sectors in the fourth quarter of 1996.
This was the first quarterly increase since the last quarter of 1995 -- but it was not nearly sufficient to make any inroads on the total level of unemployment.
